description: Not independently attested in folklore literature. In Philippine languages bata means 'child,' and bata-bata was a term for small carved ancestor images (taotao/anito) in pre-colonial religion; the bat-spirit narrative belongs to Udmurt tradition, not the Philippines. The closest genuine analogues are the anito and diwata guardian spirits of indigenous Philippine belief.
research_notes: Corrupted entry: Udmurt bat-spirit text pasted onto a Philippine name meaning 'child'; no such Philippine being attested. bata-bata = carved ancestor images.

description: Ancestor veneration is the foundation of Batammariba (Tamberma/Somba) religion of the Atakora Mountains in Togo and Benin. The dead dwell in earthen cone-altars within the takienta tower-houses, and the people call themselves Serpent Children of an underground Serpent Mother. Initiation rites and ritual consult the ancestors, who are held to govern the land and community.
source: Batammariba oral tradition; UNESCO Koutammakou documentation; Blier (1987)
research_notes: Real ancestor-cult tradition (Togo/Benin); corrected from a pasted Philippine 'Bata' description. The unverified 'Kumpo/Tiyebe' names from the old text were dropped.

description: The batibat is a vengeful tree-dwelling hag of Ilocano folklore, an obese female spirit who, when her tree is felled for a house post, migrates into it and sits on the chests of sleepers to suffocate them with fatal nightmares (bangungot). Biting one's thumb or wiggling the toes breaks her grip; the belief explains sudden unexplained nocturnal death syndrome.
source: Ilocano oral tradition; Ramos, Creatures of Philippine Lower Mythology
research_notes: Corrupted text described Batammariba ancestors; batibat is the well-attested Ilocano nightmare hag (Ramos 1971/1990), called bangungot in Tagalog.

description: The bauk is a bear-like bogeyman of Serbian folklore, an animal-shaped monster hiding in dark corners, holes, and abandoned houses to grab, carry away, and devour victims, especially children. It has a clumsy gait (bauljanje) and an onomatopoeic cry of 'bau,' and is driven off by light and noise. Scholars read it as folk memory of the brown bear, once widespread in the Balkans.
source: Serbian oral tradition; recorded by Vuk Karadžić
research_notes: Corrupted text described the Lithuanian Baubas; bauk is the attested Serbian bogeyman, also used for Tolkien's 'goblin' in Serbian translation.

description: The baykok (Ojibwe bakaak, 'bones draped in skin') is a malevolent skeletal spirit of Anishinaabe tradition: emaciated, translucent-skinned, with glowing red eyes, it flies through Great Lakes forests with shrill cries, hunting warriors, whom it paralyzes with invisible arrows or beats with a club before devouring their livers. It reached English literature via Longfellow's Song of Hiawatha.
research_notes: Corrupted text described the Serbian Bauk; baykok (bakaak, pa'guk) is an attested Ojibwe/Algonquin skeletal spirit, noted by Speck (1915) and others.

description: In Cree (Nehiyaw) tradition the bear is one of the most powerful animal beings, honored as a teacher, healer, and source of medicine power who shares knowledge of medicinal plants and hunting with those who approach with humility and respect. Regarded as a relative who walks between worlds, the bear guides dreamers and vision-fasters, revealing life paths during vision quests.
research_notes: Trimmed generic, repetitive spiritual prose; Cree bear reverence is real but specifics kept general and non-invented.

description: Not independently attested in folklore literature. No bear species is native to southern Africa, and Shona clan totems (mitupo) and ancestral spirits (vadzimu) draw only on native animals. The entry itself concedes this and then invents a bear role in Shona cosmology; the genuine analogues are the vadzimu ancestors and mitupo animal totems of Shona religion.
research_notes: Fabricated: admits no native bear in Zimbabwe, then invents a bear spirit role in Shona totem/ancestor cosmology. No such being documented.

description: Not independently attested in folklore literature. Muisca religion has no bear water-spirit; the figure conflated here is Nencatacoa (Nem-catacoa), the bear- or fox-shaped patron of weavers, artists, and drunken festivities on the Altiplano Cundiboyacense, recorded by chronicler Pedro Simón. He is a celebration deity, with no attested link to water or lakes such as Guatavita.
source: Muisca religion, recorded by Pedro Simón
research_notes: Conflates the real bear/fox god Nencatacoa into an invented water-spirit role; admitted 'not primarily a water spirit' in old text.

description: Not independently attested in folklore literature. 'Bears' is a generic label rather than a named being, and the entry invents a Chinook bear-spirit guardian with no specific tale or named tradition. Bears do appear in real Pacific Northwest oral traditions — as clan figures and Transformer-era characters — but no such generalized spirit is documented for the Chinook.
research_notes: Generic Chinook bear-spirit filler with no named tale or tradition; hedged animal-spirit moralizing. No single 'Bears' being attested.

description: Not independently attested in folklore literature. Only the village of Beetgum (Bitgum), Friesland, is real; no ghost or spirit named 'Beetgumer Grom' appears in Frisian folklore collections such as the Low Countries folktale bank. The murdered-farmer story is unverifiable filler. Genuine Frisian analogues include the klabautermann and regional household-sprite traditions.
research_notes: No such Frisian ghost attested; only the village name is real. Rest is generic ghost padding. Similar name 'Grom' appears only as a modern comic-book giant.

description: Not independently attested in folklore literature as a ghost. Bhand (from Sanskrit bhanda, 'jester') names the traditional folk-entertainer communities of South Asia — jesters, mimics, and storytellers, including the satirical Bhand Pather theatre of Kashmir — not a vengeful spirit. The ghost narrative is fabricated; the genuine analogues are the bhoot and churail.
research_notes: Bhand is an attested South Asian jester/folk-entertainer community (Pamment 2017), not a ghost; the vengeful-spirit description is fabricated.

description: A bhoot is the ghost of a person who died violently, prematurely, or without proper funeral rites in South and Southeast Asian folklore, remaining earthbound to haunt the site of death. Referenced in Sanskrit texts such as the Garuda Purana and familiar across Hindu, Muslim, and Buddhist cultures, bhoots are warded off with rituals, charms, and priestly intervention.
research_notes: Trimmed: several sentences restated the same cause-and-haunting concept. Kept general South/Southeast Asian bhoot facts.

description: Not independently attested in folklore literature. No named 'Bhoot of Haveli' entity exists; the description is generic haunted-mansion filler. Havelis — the grand mansions of Rajasthan, Gujarat, Punjab, and Uttar Pradesh — are real, and general bhoot lore attaches to many abandoned houses, but no specific mansion-ghost being is documented under this name.
research_notes: No attested 'Bhoot of Haveli' entity; generic haunted-mansion filler with no named source or tale. Haveli architecture itself is real.

description: Not independently attested in folklore literature. Bison are not native to the Northwest Coast, and no Kwakwaka'wakw ancestor-spirit is a bison. The Kwakwaka'wakw do hold real ancestor-founder spirits whose names, songs, and dances are potlatch privileges, but none is a bison figure; the entry invents the role through a claimed 'trade' route.
research_notes: Admits bison not native to the Kwakwaka'wakw coast, then invents a potlatch ancestor-spirit role. Potlatch founder-spirits are real, but not bison.

description: Not independently attested in folklore literature. Bison are absent from Aztec cosmology, and the entry grafts a bison spirit onto the tonal/nagual animal-companion beliefs recorded in sources like the Florentine Codex. Real Aztec animal spirits and deities — including the nagual shapeshifting and gods' animal forms — never include bison.
research_notes: No bison in Aztec cosmology; fabricated spirit grafted onto tonal/nagual companion beliefs. Wrong source_quality (was 'expert').

description: Not independently attested in folklore literature. Bison never occurred in the Andes, and the claim that they did is false; the bison spirit set among Quechua apu mountain spirits and huaca shrines is invented. Genuine Quechua animal guides and mountain/earth powers exist, but none is a bison being.
research_notes: Falsely claims bison known in South America; invented apu/huaca bison spirit. Apus and huacas are real, not bison.

description: Not independently attested in folklore literature. Bison are not native to Yurok territory on the lower Klamath River, and the entry invents a bison spirit 'known through trade' with no source. Yurok cosmology centers on the river, ocean, forest, and the Immortals who established ceremonies; no bison being appears in it.
research_notes: Admits bison not native to Yurok territory, then invents a spirit role via trade with interior tribes. No source supports it.

description: Not independently attested in folklore literature. The Baloch have no water-buffalo deity; the Hingol River drought legend and milk-pouring rituals are fabricated, and the cited Turkic/Mongol source is mismatched. Real Baloch tradition centers on Islam and saint veneration, including the Hinglaj Mata shrine on the Hingol, not on any bovine deity.
research_notes: Invented Hingol water-buffalo deity with fabricated drought legend and ribbon rituals; source mismatched. Hinglaj Mata is the real Hingol site.

description: Not independently attested in folklore literature. The Nanih Waiya emergence mound is genuine Choctaw tradition, but no Great Buffalo deity appears in Choctaw creation accounts; buffalo entered the Choctaw homeland relatively late. The agricultural bison-spirit role, hide-for-shelter migration story, and 'every part of the buffalo' teachings are invented.
research_notes: Real Nanih Waiya conflated with a fabricated Great Buffalo deity absent from Choctaw creation accounts.

description: Not independently attested in folklore literature. The White Buffalo Calf Woman (Ptesáŋ Wiŋ) and white-buffalo symbolism are genuine Lakota traditions, but no 'Bison Ghost' omen, spirit-herd return, or Black Hills haunting is documented; the 'some elders say' framing signals invention. Real Lakota spirit beings (wanagi) are not bison ghosts.
research_notes: Hedged 'some elders say' invention of a Bison Ghost built around the real White Buffalo Calf Woman theme. No such figure documented.

description: Not independently attested in folklore literature. No primordial Bison Giant exists in Lakota tradition; the creation-story of a titan whose body forms the prairies and Black Hills is fabricated. Genuine Lakota narratives concern the White Buffalo Calf Woman and the sacred beings of the Black Hills (He Sapa), none of them a land-forming bison giant.
research_notes: Fabricated primordial Bison Giant whose body forms the prairies/Black Hills; not an attested Lakota figure.

description: Not independently attested in folklore literature. Bison are not native to South America, and the volcano-dwelling, Pillan-linked bison giant is invented. Mapuche cosmology includes real ngen (masters of nature) and Pillan spirits of volcanoes and lightning, and the Nguillatun ceremony, but no bison being figures in it.
research_notes: Admits bison not native to South America, then invents a volcano-dwelling Pillan-linked giant. Pillan and ngen are real; the bison is not.

description: Not independently attested in folklore literature. The entry itself admits the spirit is a post-contact syncretic invention. Real Aztec nature powers — the tlaloqueh rain/earth spirits and Xipe Totec's renewal rites — are documented, but no bison nature-spirit appears in the Florentine Codex or other sources.
research_notes: Explicitly post-contact syncretic invention; no Aztec bison nature-spirit exists. Tlaloqueh and Xipe Totec are real.

description: Not independently attested in folklore literature. The entry concedes there were no bison in pre-Columbian Oaxaca, then invents a 'pitao of the grasslands.' Zapotec pitao are genuine deities and spirits of nature, but none is a bison figure; the mountain-shrine offering role is fabricated.
research_notes: Admits 'absence of true bison in pre-Columbian Oaxaca,' then invents a pitao bovine spirit. Pitao are real; bison is not among them.

description: Not independently attested in folklore literature. The directional, color, maize, and Chicomecoatl associations assigned to a bison are fabricated; bison were unknown in Aztec cosmology. The teotl concept and the maize goddess Chicomecoatl are real, but never linked to bison, and no post-contact cattle integration is documented.
research_notes: Fabricated Aztec directional/color/Chicomecoatl association for an animal never present in Aztec cosmology.

description: Not independently attested in folklore literature. No Creek (Muscogee) bison trickster exists; bison were marginal in the Southeast, and Creek trickster stories center on figures like Rabbit (Chukfi). The swamp-guardian, shape-shifting, and 'hard lessons' moralizing are invented with no named tradition.
research_notes: No Creek/Muscogee bison trickster attested; generic swamp-spirit moralizing with no tradition. The real Creek trickster is Chukfi the Rabbit.

description: Not independently attested in folklore literature. Bison are not native to the Andes, and the puna-dwelling, lightning-linked trickster said to herald pachakuti is invented. Pachakuti (world-turning upheaval) and mountain apus are genuine Quechua concepts, but no bison being is recorded in Quechua tradition.
research_notes: Admits bison not native to the Andes, then invents a pachakuti trickster on the puna. Pachakuti and apus are real; the bison is not.

description: Not independently attested in folklore literature. No Shona bison trickster exists; Shona trickster roles belong to the hare (Tsuro) and jackal, and the high god Mwari is served by human mediums (svikiro) at shrines, not by bison messengers. The granite-kopje illusion stories are invented.
research_notes: No Shona bison trickster; generic Mwari-cult messenger filler with invented illusions. The hare (Tsuro) is the real Shona trickster.

description: Not independently attested in folklore literature. The Nommo are genuine Dogon ancestral water spirits, but no bison spring-guardian is recorded among them, and bison play no role in Dogon cosmology. The Bandiagara spring-keeper story is invented.
research_notes: Real Nommo lore hijacked to fabricate a bison spring-guardian absent from Dogon tradition. Nommo are real; bison is not.

description: Not independently attested in folklore literature. The entry itself describes the spirit as a fusion invented around the bison. Chaac is a genuine Maya rain deity but is never depicted with or served by a bison; the oceanic steed, Venus-link, and calendar-round associations are fabricated.
research_notes: Explicitly 'born from the fusion of Maya water mythology with the symbolism of the bison'; invented Chaac steed.

description: Not independently attested in folklore literature. No pike spirit named 'Blak' exists in Finnish mythology. The description grafts an invented name onto the genuine Kalevala motif of the giant pike whose jawbone Väinämöinen used to make the first kantele; that pike is not a named, personalized being.
research_notes: No 'Blak' pike spirit exists in Finnish mythology; invented name grafted onto the real Kalevala kantele-pike story.

description: The bluecap is a mine spirit of the Northumberland and Durham coalfields (Anglo-Scottish border), seen as a small blue flame that worked as a supernatural putter hauling loaded coal tubs. It expected a putter's wage left in a corner, accepting no more or less, and could lead miners to rich seams or warn of cave-ins. At Shilbottle Colliery it was also called the Blue Bonnet.
source: English mining folklore; Colliery Guardian (1863); Briggs, An Encyclopedia of Fairies
research_notes: Trimmed wordy text and redundant English/Scottish contrast plus template filler line; kept putter/wages/cave-in facts.

description: In the mining folklore of the Anglo-Scottish borders, the bluecap is a mine spirit of the brownie kind, appearing as a small blue flame that moved loaded coal tubs like a putter. Treated with respect and paid its due wages, it helped miners; cheated, it withheld its aid. Scottish and English pitmen shared the tradition along the border coalfields.
source: Border mining folklore; Henderson, Notes on the Folk-Lore of the Northern Counties
research_notes: Old text was a verbatim copy of the England entry; rewritten as the shared Anglo-Scottish border mine-spirit tradition.

description: Not independently attested in folklore literature as a water serpent. The name (feminine of boiadeiro, 'cattle driver') labels the real Brazilian class of cowboy spirits — the Boiadeiros of Umbanda and the bumba-meu-boi ox-festival tradition — but the great black serpent described is the Cobra Grande/Boiúna of Amazonian legend, mislabeled here.
source: Brazilian folklore; Umbanda Boiadeiro tradition; bumba-meu-boi
research_notes: Conflation: the great black serpent legend (Boiúna/Cobra Grande) mislabeled as 'Boiadeira,' the real ox-cowboy figure. No 'Boiadeira' serpent attested.

description: Buda (Ge'ez: ቡዳ) is the Eritrean-Ethiopian belief in the evil eye wielded by hereditary social groups, often metalworkers, potters, and tanners, who harm others through their gaze and are said to shapeshift into hyenas at night. Protective amulets (kitab), holy water, and invocations of God's name ward off its effects.
research_notes: Accurate attested evil-eye/hyena-shifter belief; removed redundant template filler ending ('known among the Eritrea people').

description: Cannibal giants are man-eating monsters of the oral traditions of Algonquian and Athabaskan peoples of Canada's Subarctic and northern woodlands — known as wihtikow (windigo) among Cree, Ojibwe, and related nations. Frozen, famine-driven giants born of isolation and starvation, they embody the dangers of the deep winter bush; related beings include the Mi'kmaq chenoo.
research_notes: Real windigo-type archetype; removed generic filler and template ending ('known among the Canada people').

description: Not independently attested in folklore literature as spirit beings. 'Canyon People' (Tseyi Ndee) is the name of an Apache band, not a class of guardian spirits; the entry invents deep-gorge inhabitants and ancestor-mediator roles with no named narrative. Genuine Apache place-spirits exist in oral tradition, but none is recorded under this name.
research_notes: 'Canyon People' is an Apache band/clan name (Tseyi Ndee), not spirit beings; generic guardian-spirit lore invented.

description: Not independently attested in folklore literature. No Trinidadian spirit named 'Carival' exists; the entry is a fabricated personification of Carnival. Trinidad's real folk entities include the douen, La Diablesse, the soucouyant, and Papa Bois, none of which is a personification of the festival.
source: none; Trinidadian folklore (douen, La Diablesse, soucouyant)
research_notes: No such Trinidadian spirit exists; a fabricated personification of Carnival with no folk tradition.

description: Not independently attested in folklore literature. No Cypriot vampire called 'Charonda' is recorded. The name speculatively conflates Charos (Charon), the Greek folk personification of death prominent in Cypriot laments, with the vrykolakas vampire tradition; no blood-drinking being of this name is documented in Cypriot sources.
research_notes: No record of a Cypriot vampire 'Charonda'; speculative conflation of Charon/Charos with vrykolakas. Charos is the real death figure.
